Acne is a common skin condition that mainly affects the face, chest, and back. It happens when the pores (tiny openings on the skin) become clogged with oil, dead skin cells, and bacteria. In many people, acne comes and goes as the skin goes through changes, especially during puberty, but it can also develop in adults.

The main causes of acne are over‑production of oil (sebum) by the sebaceous glands, a buildup of skin cells inside the pores, and the growth of bacteria called *Cutibacterium acnes* (formerly *Propionibacterium acnes*). Factors such as hormonal fluctuations, stress, certain medications, and even diet can influence how much oil the skin makes and how quickly clogged pores develop.

If you’re concerned about your acne or if it’s persistent, mild, or severe, a dermatologist can recommend safe options such as gentle cleansers, topical treatments that contain benzoyl peroxide, salicylic acid, or retinoids, and sometimes oral medications for more stubborn cases. A brain tumor is an abnormal growth of cells that forms inside the brain.  
Unlike other cancers that spread to other organs, a brain tumor usually expands locally, pushing on nearby structures such as nerves, blood vessels, or brain tissue. Because the brain controls everything from movement to speech to memory, even a small tumor can produce noticeable problems.

People with brain tumors may experience symptoms such as headaches that don’t improve with rest, problems with balance or walking, difficulty speaking or swallowing, changes in mood or personality, or vision or hearing disturbances. Children may have vomiting, seizures, or developmental delays. The specific symptoms depend on where in the brain the tumor is located and how fast it grows.

Diagnosis is made with imaging studies (MRI or CT scans) and sometimes a biopsy that removes a small tissue sample for laboratory testing. Once the type and size of the tumor are known, doctors plan treatment. In many cases the first step is surgical removal if the tumor can be removed safely. Other options can include radiation therapy, chemotherapy, or targeted drugs, as well as supportive care to manage symptoms.

The goal of treatment is to control or remove the tumor while preserving brain function as much as possible. Because each case is unique, a team of neurologists, neurosurgeons, oncologists, radiation specialists, and other professionals work together to create a personalized care plan.
